cards.front: What three properties make arrays special?
cards.back: Efficiency, compile-time type checking, and the ability to hold primitives
cards.extra: An array is a linear block with O(1) indexed access and a fixed length. Generics give containers the type checking; autoboxing fakes the primitives.
cards.example:
int[] a = new int[2]; // holds primitives, fast indexed access
a[0] = 1;
// a[1] = "x"; // does not compile: element type checked at compile time
System.out.println(a[0] + " " + a.length);

cards.front: What happens when you index past the end of an array?
cards.extra: The check is on every access — that is part of what you pay for the safety. It is a RuntimeException, so the compiler will not force a catch.
cards.example:
int[] a = new int[2];
try { a[2] = 1; } catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e) { System.out.println("past the end"); }

cards.back: An array whose elements are references to arrays
cards.extra: Rows can differ in length, and the outer array can hold null rows. Nothing about the type forces a rectangular shape.
cards.example:
int[][] rows = new int[2][];
rows[0] = new int[]{1, 2};
rows[1] = new int[]{3};
System.out.println(rows[0].length + " " + rows[1].length); // two arrays referenced by rows

cards.front: Which utility class provides fill, sort, binarySearch and equals for arrays?
cards.extra: All static, all type-specific overloads. Arrays.toString is the quickest way to see an array's contents in a log.
cards.example:
int[] a = new int[3];
java.util.Arrays.fill(a, 7);
java.util.Arrays.sort(a);
System.out.println(java.util.Arrays.binarySearch(a, 7) + " " + java.util.Arrays.equals(a, new int[]{7, 7, 7}));

cards.front: When should you still choose an array over an ArrayList?
cards.back: When the size is fixed and you need raw speed or primitive storage
cards.extra: An ArrayList boxes primitives and grows by copying. The book's rule is: prefer containers, keep arrays for performance-critical, fixed-size cases.
cards.example:
int[] a = new int[3]; // fixed size, primitive storage
a[0] = 1; // direct indexed access: fast, no boxing
System.out.println(a[0] + " " + a.length);
